The Yamnaya expansion was the spread of herders of the Yamnaya culture out of the Pontic Caspian steppe, north of the Black and Caspian seas, from about 3300 BCE. Their name comes from the Russian word for pit, after the pit graves they dug under burial mounds called kurgans.

The Yamnaya lived mostly on cattle and sheep. They moved with their herds in wheeled wagons, which let them live on the open grassland far from rivers. Whether they also rode horses is still argued; true horse domestication came a little later on the same steppe.

Ancient DNA has made the Yamnaya one of the big stories of recent archaeology. Their descendants moved both ways:

  • West into Europe, where people of the Corded Ware culture carry a large share of steppe ancestry. In a few centuries much of the population of northern and central Europe changed.
  • East to the Altai mountains, in the Afanasievo culture.

Most linguists link the Yamnaya to Proto-Indo-European, the ancestor of languages from English and Greek to Persian and Hindi. The steppe herders who came after them, the Sintashta and Andronovo cultures, are tied to the Indo-Iranian branch, and later to the Indo-Aryan migrations into South Asia.

The link between genes, pots and languages is a strong theory, not a proven fact. But few events on this chart have left a bigger mark on who lives where and what they speak.
